expansion: The dendritic ulcer is the classic epithelial presentation of herpes simplex keratitis, and the lecture states this contraindication as a named clinical pearl: "NEVER use topical steroids in EPITHELIAL herpes keratitis – this promotes viral replication and can result in corneal perforation" (L15,16, page 16), repeated later as "HSV epithelial: dendritic ulcer with terminal buds → NO steroids" (L15,16, page 16). Because active viral replication in the epithelium is the driving process in a dendritic ulcer, suppressing the local immune response with a steroid removes the check on that replication and risks progression to a geographic ulcer or perforation, exactly as the lecture's worked scenario states: "Correct Answer: Topical antiviral... NO TOPICAL STEROIDS" for a dendritic ulcer case (L15,16, page 16). A catarrhal (marginal) ulcer is an immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to staphylococcal antigens, and the lecture's treatment for it explicitly includes topical steroids alongside blepharitis treatment: "treat blepharitis + topical steroids" (L15,16, page 16), so steroids are not contraindicated there. A shield ulcer is not covered in this cornea lecture; it is a sterile epithelial defect from mechanical rubbing of giant papillae in vernal keratoconjunctivitis, and topical steroids are part of its standard management to control the underlying allergic inflammation (not taken from the course material). A fascicular ulcer is a peripheral corneal ulcer that migrates centrally, most often bacterial or associated with vascularisation, and it is not linked anywhere in the lecture to a steroid contraindication, since the deck's steroid warnings are specifically tied to active herpetic epithelial replication (not taken from the course material). Only the dendritic (herpetic epithelial) ulcer carries the lecture's explicit steroid contraindication.
objective: Identify the dendritic (herpetic epithelial) corneal ulcer as the one where topical steroids are contraindicated
